newsitem.title: UK: CBI against changes in UK corporation tax.
newsitem.headline: CBI against changes in UK corporation tax.

text.p: Britain's top employers organisation the Confederation of British Industry on Wednesday welcomed parts of Gordon Brown's first budget but expressed concern about changes to corporation tax.

"Today's budget reflects the need for modest fiscal tightening and contains a number of measures business can support," said Adair Turner, the CBI's director-general. "But one measure -- the radical change to the corporation tax regime -- we do not support."
Brown, in his first budget, cut corporation tax by two percentage points to 31 percent, backdated to April 1997.
That encouraged the stock market but only until he said he was abolishing tax credits paid to pension funds and other institutions through the Advanced Corporation Tax structure.
That means the major institutions -- which are exempt from ACT and therefore claim it back as a credit on shares they own -- will have less of an incentive to hold UK equities.

"The budget includes a welcome reduction in both mainstream and smaller firm rates of corporation tax," Turner said. "But the benefit of this change is likely to be more than offset by the immediate abolition of dividend tax credit payments and by planned changes to the imputation tax system."
A change as significant as that should only have come after proper consultation, he said.
On a more positive note, Turner welcomed Brown's focus on economic stability and sound finances and said the moderate measures taken to rein in consumer demand were in line with CBI recommendations.
"On public expenditure, the CBI fully supports the commitment to existing total spending targets and the priority given to funding in education," he added.
Brown confirmed he would match the spending targets of the previous government for two years but still found an extra 2.3 billion pounds to spend on education in fiscal 1998/99.
The only other thorny issue for British employers was the windfall tax on privatised utilities. But everybody knew that was coming.

"While the CBI has opposed the principle of the retrospective windfall tax, the clear commitment that it will be one-off is important and we are pleased that the amount raised will not exceed market expectations," Turner said.
Brown said he would raise a net 4.8 billion stg from the utilities including a gas levy. Most of that will go to fund Labour's "Welfare-to-Work" programme.
